Peer-to-peer wallet

People split dinner by sending each other money from their phones. A transfer takes money from one balance and adds it to another, and the sender must see the new balance right away. A flaky mobile connection often makes the app send the same transfer twice. Practise this medium system design problem for free, with no sign-up.

Play this problem

The brief

People split dinner by sending each other money from their phones. A transfer takes money from one balance and adds it to another, and the sender must see the new balance right away. A flaky mobile connection often makes the app send the same transfer twice.

Think of a wallet app like Venmo.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
600,000 active people a month
Audience in plain numbers
600,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 2,500 requests per second
Request mix
Read: 50%; Payment: 20%; Sign-in: 10%; Write: 10%; Notification: 10%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Read: ≈ 700 ms; Payment: ≈ 800 ms; Sign-in: ≈ 1,000 ms; Write: ≈ 700 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $9,800
Data at rest
≈ 3 TB
Where users are
North America: 100%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Read: 900 seconds; Payment: 3,600 seconds; Sign-in: 900 seconds; Write: 3,600 seconds; Notification: 900 seconds
Fresh reads
People must see their own changes. At most 0.1% of reads may be stale in the model.
Personal reads
90% of reads are private; a shared public copy cannot answer them.
Required proofs
Audit trail; Managed encryption keys; Signed-in access

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • Money is counted in cents, never in decimals.
  • Transfers settle between balances inside the wallet.
  • Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

Questions that shape the design

Can a balance ever be wrong, even for a second?

The sender must always see their own latest balance. Other people can wait a moment.

What if the phone loses signal after tapping Send?

The app retries with the same transfer key. The money must move once.

What does a regulator ask for?

A tamper-proof record of every transfer, encryption, and proof that every action was a signed-in user.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 12:00 · Duplicate delivery

    The queue redelivers 1 percent of messages. Without protection, some customers are charged twice.

    Affected share: 1%. Duration: ≈ 3,600 seconds.

  2. 16:00 · Compliance audit

    An auditor checks your design: who did what, encryption keys, personal data, backups and consent.

  3. 20:30 · Database failover

    The primary database dies. A standby takes over after about a minute.

    Duration: ≈ 60 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • A reader may use a copy that is a moment behind. Which reads in this app must never do that?
  • Conserve funds with atomic, unique transfers under concurrent spending.
  • No cache on balances means every balance read hits the ledger. It costs more database and avoids ever showing a stale balance after a transfer.
  • Sync replication adds a few milliseconds to each transfer and guarantees a failover loses nothing. Async would be faster and could drop the last second of transfers.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Which copy is the truth
  • Exactly once, on purpose
  • Proof built in

Related problems

  • Hard

    Bank ledger

    You run the system of record for a regional bank: every deposit, withdrawal and card settlement is a posting that must be exact and permanent. Customers in two continents read balances all day, and regulators can ask for proof at any time. A bad day for you is a loss of even one posting.

  • Hard

    Crypto exchange

    People trade coins, check prices and withdraw funds around the clock from every continent. A sudden price crash makes everyone log in and trade at once, attackers flood you hoping to knock the site over, and a leaked key could empty a wallet. Balances must never be wrong.

  • Hard

    Airline booking

    You run the booking system for an airline. Fare searches are heavy, seats are limited, and every flight needs the right number of tickets, no more and no fewer. You depend on a partner system for fares from other airlines, and it has strict limits. A fare sale and a slow partner will both happen on the same day.

  • Easy

    Invoicing and billing

    Small businesses create invoices, email them to customers and take card payments online. On the last working day of the month everyone sends and chases invoices at once. Nobody may get the same invoice email twice, and no invoice may vanish.
